title.en: Apply symmetry operations to labelled elements

summary: Represent each symmetry as a permutation of identified features and compose operations in a stated order.
objective: Make a symmetry demonstration exact enough that composition, inverses and closure can be checked.
applies_when: A shape is acted on by rotations, reflections or other symmetry operations.
Operations are composed, or a sequence is built up by the viewer.
The scene talks about a symmetry group, its order or its structure.
intent_signals: show the symmetries of the square
example_prompts: Show that these two symmetry operations do not commute.
Let me build a sequence of symmetries and see the resulting permutation.
negative_signals: Visual symmetry used as decoration with no algebraic claim.
Approximate or statistical symmetry in organic forms.
not_for: Visual symmetry used as decoration with no algebraic claim.
Approximate or statistical symmetry in organic forms.

principles: A symmetry operation is only observable through features it actually moves, and the chosen feature set must separate the operations you want to distinguish. Marking only the centre of a square distinguishes nothing, since every symmetry fixes it; a set of features is adequate only if the action on it is faithful, meaning no non-identity operation leaves every marker in place. A continuous rotational symmetry cannot be represented by any finite marker set at all.

Composition has a direction. Applying one operation and then another is a specific convention, and the inverse of a sequence reverses it, so the inverse of doing three operations in order is undoing them from the last backwards.
The set of symmetries is closed: composing two of them yields another symmetry of the same object, which is what makes the resulting sequence expressible as a single permutation.
Presenting the result as disjoint cycles compresses a sequence into the structure that actually matters, which is where each labelled feature ends up.
implementation: Label the features the operations permute, such as vertices, faces or edge markers, and keep the labels visible during motion.

Store the current group element itself, and use the marker permutation as its display. Where the marker action is faithful the two agree; where it is not, the element remains authoritative and the markers alone cannot reconstruct it.
State the composition convention on screen and keep it consistent between the visual sequence and the algebraic readout.
Provide an inverse control that composes the reversed inverse sequence rather than restoring a remembered pose.
Show the cycle structure of the accumulated element so the algebra and the picture are the same object.
observable_checks: Where the group has a non-commuting pair, compose it in both orders and confirm the results differ. An abelian symmetry group, such as the rotations of a shape with no reflection symmetry, has no such pair and is not thereby faulty; check instead that composition matches the stated multiplication.
Apply an operation and its inverse and confirm the permutation returns exactly to the identity.
Compose any two operations and confirm the result is in the stated set, which tests closure.
Check the displayed cycle notation against the visible positions of the labelled features.

Apply each non-identity operation and confirm at least one marker moves; if any operation leaves every marker fixed, the feature set is not faithful and the permutation readout is not the group element.

creative_affordances: Labels can be colours, glyphs, textures or small objects; only their distinctness matters.
Abstract or ornamental subjects work as well as regular polygons when their features are identified.
A motion trail, an orientation gnomon or an asymmetric ornament can distinguish intermediate rotations without colouring every feature individually.
known_limits: Authored guidance citing composition and inverse conventions from a puzzle-oriented group theory source; it proves no group-theoretic result here.
It does not enumerate the elements of any specific symmetry group.

claims.statement: Composing two operations means applying one and then the other in a stated order, and the inverse of a sequence of operations is the sequence of their inverses applied in reverse order; any move or move sequence can be written as a product of disjoint cycles showing where each labelled piece moves.
claims.scope: Permutation composition conventions as used for puzzle and symmetry operations; it does not assert any specific group structure.

source_refs.locator: Composition of functions; inverse of a move sequence; disjoint cycle notation
